title: Fourteen million people, two million tickets
teaches: Selling scarce inventory: virtual waiting rooms, expiring holds, preventing double-selling, and mitigating bots

blocks.text: On the morning of 15 November 2022, Ticketmaster opened a presale for Taylor Swift's Eras Tour, her first tour in five years, with 52 stadium dates across the United States. The presale was meant for fans who had registered in advance and received an access code. By the company's own account two days later, about 14 million users and bots showed up. Its systems took 3.5 billion requests that day, four times their previous peak. Pages hung, queues stalled, and seats vanished from shopping baskets during payment. Ticketmaster still sold more than 2 million tickets that day, a record, and then cancelled the general public sale planned for 18 November, citing insufficient remaining inventory to meet demand.[^senate]

Selling a scarce item to far more buyers than inventory allows is a distinct systems design problem. Most of the system's work consists of rejecting requests, and the primary invariant is that no seat may be sold twice. In this lesson, we will design a ticketing system for **14 million users and 2 million seats**, and then compare our design with the Ticketmaster outage. This same architecture applies to retail flash sales, hotel reservations for peak weekends, and ride-hailing dispatch systems matching one driver to one rider.

**Functional requirements.** The system must admit users in a fair order, display available seats, allow a buyer to hold selected seats for a limited time during checkout, sell each seat at most once, issue the ticket, and prevent automated bots and reseller scripts from exhausting the inventory.

**Non-functional requirements.** Consistency and latency requirements vary by operation. The **seat map** may be a few seconds stale, because displaying a recently taken seat as available only costs the user an extra click. A **hold** requires strict consistency, as assigning two holds to one seat is the exact failure the system exists to prevent. **Payment** must execute at most once per order, using the idempotency keys from lesson 22. Finally, the system must reject the 12 million unsuccessful users quickly and with minimal compute cost.

**Out of scope.** We will not cover dynamic pricing, secondary resale, refunds, or rendering the venue map. These features matter commercially, but they are not the bottlenecks that cause outages when a sale opens.
Before designing the architecture, we should estimate the required transaction throughput.

blocks.caption: Throughput estimates for a large ticket sale. A 5-second refresh interval approximates the behaviour of an anxious user waiting on a stalled page.
blocks.task: Estimate the write throughput for sales, then test different traffic parameters

blocks.text: Selling 2 million seats over 4 hours averages about 140 seats per second. A single relational database can easily commit 140 transactions per second. The load that overwhelms the system comes from read and status requests around the sale: 14 million users refreshing a seat map every 5 seconds generates 2.8 million requests per second, or 20,000 requests for every seat sold. The engineering challenge is not increasing write throughput for sales, but preventing 14 million clients from querying the backend simultaneously, while serving the 12 million users who will not get tickets using something much cheaper than a database query.

The seat service in the simulation below has a capacity of 160 checkout requests per second, while users arrive at a higher rate. If you route traffic directly to the seat service, the queue overflows. Instead, you can place a **waiting room** in front of the service to buffer incoming traffic and admit users at a fixed rate of 140 users per second. In this simulation, each admitted user makes a single checkout request, so an admission rate of 140 users per second leaves a headroom of 20 requests per second for retries and latency spikes. In a production system, a user makes multiple requests (loading the seat map, placing a hold, and submitting payment), so you would set the admission rate to the service's capacity divided by the average number of requests per user, minus a 10% to 20% safety margin. The simulation runs at reduced speed with high network latency so you can observe individual requests.

blocks.caption: Clients, an optional waiting room, the seat service, and the seats database table. Without a waiting room, a client whose request times out after 3 seconds retries up to two times. Amber dots above a component represent queued requests.
blocks.task: Handle an arrival rate of 400 or more users per second using a waiting room

blocks.text: When 400 users per second bypass the waiting room, requests arrive at the seat service faster than it can process them. Within seconds, the queueing delay exceeds the 3-second client timeout. Clients time out and send retry requests, increasing the queue length further while the service spends its CPU cycles processing requests for clients that have already disconnected. Although CPU utilisation stays at 100%, effective throughput (goodput) drops near zero right when demand peaks.[^metastable] With a waiting room in place, the seat service receives traffic strictly within its capacity and processes sales at a steady rate of 140 seats per second. The queue moves to the waiting room, where holding connections is cheap and the system can report queue positions to users.

A waiting room scales cheaply because it performs minimal computation per user. Upon arrival, a client receives a **signed token** containing their queue identifier and timestamp. The client views a static HTML page served from a content delivery network (lesson 19), which polls a lightweight endpoint every 30 seconds to check if their token's number has been reached. The waiting room admits tokens at the seat service's capacity rate using a token bucket algorithm (as covered in lesson D1, *Saying no politely*). Once admitted, the token grants temporary access to the seat map. To prevent users from gaining an advantage by arriving hours early or opening thousands of browser tabs, the system collects all tokens issued before the sale starts and shuffles them into a **random order** at the opening timestamp. In a multi-region deployment, a central coordinator shuffles the pre-sale tokens across all regions once, and each regional waiting room admits users from its assigned partition of the global list.

A system should reject invalid requests as early and cheaply as possible. For an invite-only presale, the edge servers validate the invitation code before issuing a waiting room token, before the request ever reaches the seat service. The edge layer also enforces per-account and per-card rate limits (lesson D1). Stateless edge servers should filter out any request that can be rejected without querying the core database.

The database schema uses one row per seat, with a composite primary key of (event, section, seat), alongside **state**, **holder**, and **hold_until** columns. The API exposes two endpoints. **POST /holds** accepts the event ID, the requested seat IDs, and an idempotency key, returning either a hold ID with an expiration timestamp or a rejection. **POST /orders** accepts the hold ID, a payment token, and a second idempotency key, charges the payment method, and converts the hold into a completed sale. Because a buyer needs time to enter payment details, a hold must last for several minutes and expire automatically if the buyer abandons the checkout. Engineers set the hold duration based on payment latency percentiles: if 99% of checkouts complete within 4 minutes, a 10-minute hold accommodates almost all buyers, while an active payment awaiting a slow bank response can extend the hold once via an additional conditional write.

A naive implementation checks seat availability by reading the seat row, verifying that the state is free, and writing the new holder ID. Consider what happens when two buyers request the same seat simultaneously through two different application servers.

blocks.caption: Two buyers request seat 14C simultaneously through two application servers connected to a shared seats table. Blue dots represent read requests, green dots represent responses, orange dots represent writes, and red dots indicate a rejected write or a double sale.
blocks.task: Run the simulation using a concurrency control mechanism that prevents double-selling

blocks.text: The read-then-write pattern fails due to a race condition: both application servers read the row before either write commits, so both observe the seat as *free*. To fix this, we combine the check and the update into an atomic **conditional write**. The query instructs the database to set the holder to the current buyer and the expiration time to 10 minutes in the future *only if* the seat currently has no holder or its existing hold has expired. In SQL, this is an UPDATE statement with the state and expiration checks in the WHERE clause. The database executes the update atomically and returns the number of modified rows: 1 row for the winning request, and 0 rows for any concurrent requests. This approach avoids holding long-lived database locks while a user types their credit card details, and abandoned holds free themselves automatically because subsequent conditional writes treat expired holds as available. To prevent clock drift between application servers from corrupting hold durations (lesson 20), the query evaluates expiration timestamps against the database server's internal clock.[^clock]

A buyer requesting four adjacent seats requires an all-or-nothing allocation, so the application wraps the four conditional writes in a single database transaction. If we partition the seats table by (event, section), adjacent seats always reside on the same database shard. The transaction executes locally on one machine without requiring a distributed two-phase commit (lesson 20). However, popular sections create hot shards, as thousands of buyers target the same few hundred rows when the sale opens. To eliminate lock contention on the database, we can route all requests for a given section to a single dedicated worker process. This section owner queues requests in memory, allocates seats sequentially, and writes the decisions to the database. Because the process holds the section's exact state in memory, it can also automatically assign the best available adjacent seats, rather than forcing users to click specific seats on a map that is already stale. If a section owner process crashes, the cluster reassigns its sections to another worker, using the same failover pattern as the chat servers in lesson D2 (*Half a billion people, a few dozen engineers*). The new owner loads the current seat states from the database, while conditional writes prevent a paused old owner from overwriting newer allocations.

Payment follows the hold. The order call charges the card with an idempotency key (lesson 22), then turns the hold into a sale with one more conditional write, *only where* this buyer still holds the seat. If the hold expired while the bank took its time, the sale write changes zero rows and the charge is refunded; better designs mark the hold *paying* when the card is submitted, so it can't expire mid-payment.

blocks.title: The consistency each operation needs
points: Seat map: serving cached data that is a few seconds stale is acceptable.
Hold: enforce a single buyer per seat using an atomic conditional write that checks for expired holds.
Payment: guarantee at-most-once charging per order using an idempotency key.
Sale: conditional on still holding the seat.

parts.title: Bot mitigation, fairness, and related systems

blocks.text: Automated scalping scripts execute HTTP requests much faster than human users, so effective bot mitigation imposes a validation cost on every participant that is negligible for a single human but expensive to run at scale. Advance registration with identity verification filters who can enter the waiting room. Binding waiting room tokens to the authenticated account and client device prevents operators from transferring tokens from a harvesting cluster to checkout scripts. Enforcing purchasing limits per account, payment card, and billing address caps the inventory any single actor can acquire. Requiring a cryptographic proof-of-work challenge or interactive puzzle at the waiting room entrance costs a human user one second of compute time, but forces a botnet operator to pay for significant CPU capacity. Finally, asynchronous post-sale audits can identify and cancel orders that reuse credit cards or physical addresses across multiple accounts.

This architecture generalises to other high-contention inventory systems. An e-commerce **flash sale** for 10,000 identical items does not require a database row per item; instead, it uses an inventory counter decremented via a conditional write checking that the count remains at 0 or above. Under a load of tens of thousands of requests per second, a single counter row becomes a database bottleneck, so engineers shard the inventory into ten counters of 1,000 items across separate database instances and route buyers to a shard at random.[^split] Similarly, a **hotel reservation system** maintains an availability counter per room type for each calendar night. A **ride-hailing service** models each available driver as a single seat: dispatching a ride offer executes a conditional write changing the driver's state from *available* to *offered to rider 7 until 12:00:15*. If the driver does not accept within 15 seconds, the hold expires automatically, ensuring the platform never assigns the same driver to two riders simultaneously.

parts.title: The Ticketmaster outage and scaling further

blocks.text: In its post-incident statement, Ticketmaster reported that traffic far exceeded capacity projections, driven largely by bot attacks and millions of uninvited users without presale codes, forcing engineers to throttle admission rates and pause queues to prevent a total outage. Ticketmaster's architecture already used the standard components from our design: a virtual waiting room, expiring seat holds, and advance fan verification. The primary failure occurred at the edge filtering layer. Because the system allowed millions of users without valid presale codes to enter the queues and generate backend traffic, unauthenticated requests consumed capacity meant for verified buyers. When the backend seat service became overloaded, active buyers experienced expiring holds during checkout and disappearing shopping baskets: classic symptoms of requests timing out in internal queues after completing database writes, causing the client session to lose state.

**At ten times**, the answer is to keep the work proportional to seats, not to people. Every check that can be done at the edge, without state, is done there: the invite code, the token's signature, the rate limit. The seat map is a cached picture refreshed every second or two from a stream of seat changes (lesson 16), never a query per viewer. Each event's seats live in their own cell (lesson 23), so one sale's trouble can't reach another's.

**At a hundred times**, or with demand that can't be predicted at all, the fair answer changes from a queue to a **lottery**: register over a week, draw winners, and give each winner a time slot with a guaranteed seat. The load becomes a scheduled trickle, bots gain nothing by speed, and nobody waits for hours to be told no. The cost is the thrill, and some buyers' sense that being early should count.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on selling something scarce
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Two million seats sell over about 4 hours, and 14 million people try to buy them. What is the main systems design problem?
choices: Recording sales fast enough, since one database cannot keep up with a stadium's worth of seats
Keeping millions of people from querying the backend at once, and rejecting most of them cheaply
Storing the seat map, which is too large for any single server to keep in memory
items.why: Writing the sales requires about 140 transactions per second, which a single database easily handles. The bottleneck comes from read traffic: millions of users refreshing the seat map generate roughly 20,000 requests per seat sold.

items.ask: A seat service is overloaded and every request sits in its queue longer than the client timeout. Why can its completed sales fall almost to zero while its CPU utilisation remains at 100%?
choices: It spends its CPU cycles processing timed-out requests for clients that have already disconnected
Its database locks every seat row during the overload, so no sale can be written until the load falls
Its machines slow their system clocks under heavy load, so every hold it has granted appears to expire at once
items.why: Compute spent on timed-out requests is wasted, and each timeout triggers a client retry that adds to the queue. A waiting room that limits admission to the service's processing capacity ensures every request completes before the client times out.

items.ask: Two application servers each read seat 14C as free, and then both write their own buyer as the holder. What is the fix?
choices: Have the application servers check each other's recent writes before confirming a hold to a buyer
Read the seat row twice before writing, so a change made in between will be noticed
Use an atomic conditional write: set the holder only where there is no current holder or the hold has expired
items.why: The race condition occurs in the gap between the read and the subsequent write. An atomic conditional write combines the state check and the update into a single database operation, modifying 1 row for the winning request and 0 rows for the losing request.

items.ask: Why does a seat hold use an expiration timestamp rather than a lock that the client explicitly releases when checkout finishes?
choices: Expiration timestamps use less storage than locks do in most relational databases, which matters for millions of seats
A self-expiring hold automatically frees the seat if the buyer closes their browser or abandons checkout
An expiration timestamp lets two buyers share the hold, so that whichever of them pays first gets the seat
items.why: An explicit lock held by a client that disconnects or closes its browser tab would leave the seat locked indefinitely. Checking hold_until in the conditional write's WHERE clause allows subsequent queries to treat an expired hold as available.

items.ask: Everyone who arrives in the waiting room before a sale opens is shuffled into a random order at the opening timestamp. What does this achieve?
choices: It spreads the database writes evenly across all of the shards that hold the event's seats
It removes the need for a waiting room
Arriving hours early, or opening many browser tabs, gives no one an advantage when the queue opens
items.why: First come, first served rewards whoever can arrive earliest and most often, which is what scripts do best.

items.ask: A flash sale has 10,000 identical items and tens of thousands of purchase attempts per second. Which database design prevents the inventory count from becoming a write bottleneck?
choices: One row per item; each buyer claims the lowest-numbered available row with a conditional write
Ten counters of 1,000 items on different shards, each decremented conditionally only if it remains at 0 or above
One counter read by each buyer and decremented by the application server once payment succeeds
items.why: One counter is a hot key, and so is "the lowest free row", which every buyer aims at. Splitting the count over shards spreads attempts, and the condition stops each going below zero. Reading then decrementing in the app would oversell.

items.ask: A ride-hailing service must never offer the same driver to two riders at once. Which dispatch design uses the same concurrency pattern as a seat hold?
choices: A conditional write setting the driver's state to offered, with an expiration timestamp a few seconds in the future
A database lock on the driver's row held until the trip ends, released by the driver's app when the rider exits the vehicle
A first-in, first-out queue of riders assigned to each individual driver
items.why: A ride dispatch offer acts just like a seat hold: one atomic conditional write succeeds while concurrent attempts modify 0 rows, and the short expiration timestamp frees the driver if they do not accept the trip.

summary: **Most of the system's work is rejecting traffic.** Selling 2 million seats over 4 hours requires only 140 write transactions per second, whereas 14 million users refreshing a page generates millions of read requests per second.

**Match consistency guarantees to each operation.** The seat map can be served stale from a cache, placing a hold requires strict atomic consistency, payment processing requires idempotency keys, and finalising the sale requires a conditional check on the hold.
**Unbuffered overload causes goodput to collapse.** When queueing delay exceeds client timeouts, servers spend 100% of their CPU cycles on abandoned requests while client retries amplify the load.

**A waiting room throttles admission to match backend capacity.** Issue cryptographically signed tokens, serve a static waiting page from a CDN, and regulate admission into the checkout service with a token bucket.
**Reject invalid traffic at the stateless edge.** Validate invitation codes, token signatures, and per-account rate limits at the edge before requests consume backend database capacity.
**Prevent double-selling with atomic conditional writes.** Update the seat holder in a single SQL statement only where the seat has no holder or the existing hold has expired.

**Use self-expiring holds evaluated against the database clock.** Including an expiration timestamp in the conditional write automatically reclaims abandoned seats without requiring background cleanup jobs or distributed locks.
**Partition seats by event and section.** A group's seats share a shard, and a single owner per hot section can allocate in memory.

**The same concurrency patterns apply to any scarce inventory.** Use sharded conditional counters for retail flash sales, per-night counters for hotel rooms, and short-lived expiring holds for ride-hailing driver dispatch.

senate.title: A Senate hearing
senate.text: The presale outage prompted an investigation by the United States Senate: its Judiciary Committee held a hearing on ticketing competition on 24 January 2023, where Live Nation Entertainment's president and CFO, Joe Berchtold, attributed much of the disruption to an unprecedented bot attack.

metastable.title: Metastable failures
metastable.text: A system that remains in a degraded state even after the initial traffic spike subsides is experiencing a **metastable** failure. Request timeouts trigger client retries, the retries keep the server queues saturated, and the saturated queues cause new requests to time out. The system can recover only if incoming load drops well below capacity long enough for the queues to drain, which is why shedding load at the edge or throttling admission with a waiting room is necessary.

clock.title: Database clock authority
clock.text: If each application server compared hold_until against its local system clock, an application server with a clock drifting 30 seconds fast would treat active holds as expired and reassign seats while the original buyers were still submitting payment. Evaluating timestamps using the database's internal clock (such as calling now() inside the SQL statement) establishes a single time authority for all conditional writes. Setting hold durations to 10 minutes also ensures that minor clock skew between client countdown timers and the database remains harmless.

split.title: Sharding an inventory counter
split.text: When inventory is partitioned across ten sharded counters, a buyer routed to an exhausted shard must retry against remaining shards before the system reports that the item is sold out, which adds a few extra internal requests as the final items sell. Alternatively, workers can dynamically reallocate inventory from a central database pool to individual shard counters as they deplete.
